title: Capacity Observability and Recovery Playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This playbook describes the observability and automated/operational responses we use to protect SLOs by managing capacity and error-budget consumption in real time. It bridges dashboards, alerting, automated mitigation, and human runbooks so teams can recover gracefully from traffic surges, model regressions, and infrastructure degradation while minimizing customer impact.

Scope

- Applies to all model-serving and API-facing services under Redwood's inference runtime (hosted, dedicated, private control plane endpoints).
- Covers telemetry design, realtime dashboards, automated throttles and shedding, capacity scaling triggers, and incident review hooks.
- Does not cover long-term procurement or hiring decisions — those live in capacity-planning guidances.

Goals and success criteria

- Maintain SLO compliance (primary SLOs) for 99.95% of tenants across normal traffic.
- Detect and respond to >90% of capacity-driven SLO degradations via automated mechanisms within the first 120s.
- Reduce customer-visible errors during surges by >60% compared to baseline manual-only response.

Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: eng-sre (oncall rotation)
- Runtime telemetry owner: eng-platform observability team
- Capacity automation owner: eng-infra autoscaling team
- Pager escalation: see global oncall rota page (/confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations)

SLOs and error budgets: how this playbook ties in

- Each service exposes a primary latency SLO and a correctness/availability SLO exported to the SLO registry.
- Error budget spend is computed per-SLO and fed into the capacity controller every 30s.
- Playbook principle: prioritize preserving customer-facing SLOs. When error-budget burn accelerates, trigger layered mitigations from non-disruptive to disruptive.

Telemetry and dashboards (what to build)

Critical telemetry signals (collected at 15s granularity):

- P50/P95/P99 latency per route
- Request QPS and per-tenant QPS
- Token generation rate and per-model token rate
- Error rate by class (5XX, 4XX client, model-failed, timeout)
- Queue length, queue latency, and head-of-line wait times
- GPU utilization and per-instance memory headroom
- KV cache hit rate and prefix-cache reuse
- Autoscaler state (desired/actual replicas, scale events)

Dashboard layout (single-pane):

1) Global health strip: primary SLO compliance % (last 5m), total error budget burn rate, active mitigations
2) Capacity heatmap: region x cluster utilization, free GPU headroom, burst pool remaining
3) Traffic map: top-100 tenants by QPS, per-tenant SLO risk score
4) Latency tails: per-model P99 trend with annotations for config changes
5) Incident timeline: correlated alerts, autoscale decisions, deployment rollouts

Suggested dashboard queries / alerts (examples)

- Alert A: SLO Burn Surge
  - Condition: global error budget burn rate > 10% per hour for two consecutive 1m windows
  - Severity: P1
  - Runbook: follow Automated mitigation -> Escalate if persists 5m

- Alert B: Latency Tail Spike
  - Condition: P99 latency > SLO threshold *1.8 for >90s and queue length increasing
  - Severity: P1
  - Runbook: immediate traffic shaping and autoscale review

- Alert C: Resource Starvation
  - Condition: any serving node GPU memory > 92% for >2m or OOMs observed
  - Severity: P0 (system)
  - Runbook: drain node, route traffic away, trigger emergency capacity pool

Automated response tiers (order from least to most disruptive)

Tier 0 — passive signals
- Notify SRE oncall and post to dedicated channel. Do not change traffic.

Tier 1 — non-disruptive mitigations (automated)
- Activate per-model request batching fallback with tighter size limits.
- Increase KV/prefix cache retention windows to reduce repeated compute.
- Route new tenant traffic to model-quantized variants (platform policy whitelist).

Tier 2 — active traffic shaping (automated with short TTL)
- Per-tenant soft rate limits: reduce non-critical tenant QPS by configured percentage (default 25%).
- Apply token-budget-aware request sampling for heavy embedding workloads (sample 1 in N requests).
- Enable best-effort token cutoff (response truncation) for large multimodal requests.

Tier 3 — capacity and failover (automated + human approval for long-running)
- Emergency burst from reserved capacity pool (if available).
- Cross-region routing to identical model variants under managed fallback policy.
- If no capacity available, enable graceful degradation policy: deny new sessions for non-SLA tenants, preserve sessions for tiers with contract guarantees.

Tier 4 — disruptive actions (human-led)
- Rolling rollback of recent model rollout or config change.
- Planned tenant shedding, contacting Customer Success for impacted customers.

Automated decision engine rules (summary)

- Input signals: per-SLO burn rate, queue latency trend, GPU mem utilization, autoscaler lag, model change markers (deployments).
- Decision outputs: apply tiered mitigations, annotate dashboard, open incident ticket if tier >=2 for >5m.
- Safety: require at least two independent signals before escalating to tier 2+ (e.g., burn rate + queue growth).

Capacity runbooks (step-by-step)

1) Immediate triage (first 5 minutes)
  a) Confirm correlated telemetry: SLO burn, latency tail, queue growth, node metrics.
  b) If Tier 1 mitigations haven't kicked in, trigger them from the automation console.
  c) Notify oncall, post summary in incident channel with link to dashboard.

2) Active mitigation (5–30 minutes)
  a) If tier 2 triggered: verify per-tenant shaping rules applied and affected tenant list.
  b) If autoscaler is not producing capacity within expected scale window, inspect scaling logs and scaling-agent metrics.
  c) If GPU memory OOMs present: cordon + drain nodes and remove from LB; enable emergency burst pool.

3) Stabilization (30–120 minutes)
  a) Monitor SLO compliance metrics and error-budget burn until trending down.
  b) Keep human-approved Tier 3 actions only with explicit change ticket (and rollback plan).
  c) Start incident review evidence collection: recording dashboard snapshots, autoscaler events, deployment diffs.

4) Recovery and rollback (post 2 hours)
  a) If root cause is model regression: rollback to previous model snapshot and monitor.
  b) If root cause is capacity engineering mismatch: create capacity task (owner, ETA) and update SLO/traffic contracts if needed.
  c) Communicate status and postmortem timeline to stakeholders.

Incident review hooks and artifacts

For every event where automated mitigations were applied or error budget burn >10% in 1h:
- Capture: dashboard snapshots, autoscaler events, node traces, recent deploys, rate-limit config changes, tenant list affected.
- Tag the incident with mitigation tiers used and time windows per tier.
- Required deliverable: short incident review (SIR) within 72h with timeline, root cause hypothesis, immediate fixes, and capacity remediation plan.

Operational tooling integrations (must-haves)

- Alerting platform: alerts must include executable playbook links and one-click action buttons to apply Tier 1/Tier 2 mitigations.
- Capacity controller: accepts decision inputs and returns applied-actions events for audit history.
- ChatOps: mitigation confirmation and audit trail should be posted to the incident channel automatically (with links).
- SLO registry: decision engine reads SLO thresholds and error budget windows directly.

Testing, drill and rollout guidance

- Quarterly chaos drills: simulate a synthetic P99 spike for 15m with 50% increased QPS on top-10 tenants to validate mitigation chain.
- Pre-rollout checklist: any deployment that changes model memory use must pass a synthetic stress test and autoscaler dry-run.
- Runbook CI: all runbook steps and automation scripts are versioned in the runbook repo and exercised on every release pipeline for the capacity controller.

Appendix: example commands and config snippets

- Example: force Tier 1 cache extension (CLI):
  rctl capacity-cache extend --model-id m-redwood-7b --seconds 300 --reason "auto-mitigation test"

- Example: small YAML for per-tenant shaping rule (policy):
  policy: per-tenant-shape
  tenant_selector: "tier != enterprise"
  qps_reduction_pct: 25
  ttl_seconds: 600

- Suggested retention of telemetry for post-incident review: full-resolution (15s) for 7d, aggregated 1m for 30d, 5m for 90d.
